newsitem.title: RUSSIA: New Russian cabinet meets, Yeltsin at U.S. summit.
newsitem.headline: New Russian cabinet meets, Yeltsin at U.S. summit.

text.p: Russia's reshuffled cabinet, under pressure to defuse rising social tensions and jump-start stalled economic reforms, held its first meeting on Thursday as President Boris Yeltsin left for a summit meeting in Helsinki.

Yeltsin headed for talks with U.S. President Bill Clinton able to count on strong support from political opponents in parliament for his campaign to halt NATO's eastward expansion, the issue expected to dominate the two-day summit.

The communist-dominated State Duma lower house of parliament had been due to debate a non-binding anti-NATO resolution declaring Russia would never become part of the western bloc. But deputies decided to hold the discussions over until Friday.
They also postponed a planned debate on an emotional call to Yeltsin not to move the mummified corpse of Bolshevik leader Vladimir Lenin from its mausoleum on Red Square.
There is little agreement over the big economic problems confronting the country.
Yeltsin left behind a new-look cabinet in which young reformers have taken broad control of economic policy.

The president, firmly back at the helm after many months of illness, hopes that new first deputy premiers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsev can swiftly resolve such problems as non-payment of bills between enterprises and chronic wage delays.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin told Thursday's cabinet meeting that Chubais was well placed to tackle the problems.
"I hope that Anatoly Chubais' knowledge and experience will help us make colossal progress," Interfax news agency quoted the premier as saying.
Chernomyrdin said there would be more personnel changes in the government but added they would not be announced until after Yeltsin's return from Helsinki on Saturday.

Chernomyrdin urged his deputies and ministers to work as a single team. "There may be different opinions here at the government meetings but everyone should work as one fist to carry out decisions once they are taken," he said.

Chubais and Nemtsov have said they are committed to giving a new push to economic reform by introducing unpopular changes in the paternalistic welfare system and by scrapping many benefits granted to enterprises and whole sectors of the economy.
Nemtsov has said the painful changes the new government will have to carry out would make it appear almost "suicidal".
But Chubais said the cabinet's plans would yield visible results quite soon that would help the government, currently very unpopular, regain support.
The new cabinet will face its first big challenge on March 27, when trade unions plan to hold a nationwide day of protests.
Chernomyrdin has sent top cabinet members to regions where the situation is most tense. Chubais was due to leave for the coal-mining region of Kemerovo later on Thursday.

The cabinet also faces hostility from the Duma, which is dominated by Yeltsin's communist and ultra-nationalist foes. They have been particularly annoyed by the appointment of Chubais, whose views and past record they despise.

Chernomyrdin has been invited to appear before the Duma on Friday to explain the government changes. Despite its loud criticism, the assembly has no power to challenge the reshuffle because the prime minister himself has remained in place.

Ekho Moskvy radio said that Chernomyrdin would hold a meeting later on Thursday with leaders of parliamentary factions in which the cabinet reshuffle and the country's broader economic and social situation would be discussed.
